title: Vertigo business cards
lede: April Greiman’s business cards for the Los Angeles shop Vertigo: a letterspaced wordmark on a tilted bar, with stripes, dots, and diagonal lines that change from card to card.
summary: Four cards with “V e r t / g o” on a tilted bar, a black triangle for the V, and stripes, dots, and checks. April Greiman, 1980.

source.label: People’s Graphic Design Archive: Vertigo business cards

evidence.note: Inspected the People’s Graphic Design Archive image (901 × 1500), a black-and-white photograph of four cards, probably reproduced from a publication; the owner of the physical cards is not stated. Not stored. Colours are not visible.

styles.note: Clear example of Greiman’s California New Wave at the scale of stationery: wide letterspacing, tilted bars, and scattered geometric marks.

context: The People’s Graphic Design Archive credits the cards to April Greiman for the client Vertigo/Lynda Weinman, printed by McCoy Printing, and dates them 1980. [People’s Graphic Design Archive](https://peoplesgdarchive.org/item/3133/vertigo-business-cards).
observed: Each card carries the wordmark “Vertigo” on a tilted rectangular bar. The V is a solid black triangle, a slash replaces the i, and a black dot follows the o.
The letters of the wordmark are spaced wide apart.

The four cards have different grounds: black vertical stripes that extend past the card edge, a dark card with round holes or dots, a light card with thin diagonal lines and circles, and a card with a pattern of rounded squares.
Addresses are set in small bold grotesque, some lines tilted or letterspaced (“L o s  A n g e l e s”).
Small words such as “gifts”, “paper”, and “fashion acces.” run along diagonal lines.
interpretation: The cards turn a small identity into a system of variations: one tilted, spaced wordmark stays fixed while the surfaces change. This is the style’s move from the poster to everyday print.
borrow: Put a letterspaced wordmark on a slightly tilted solid bar.
Replace one letter with a geometric mark (a triangle, a slash, a dot).
Keep the mark fixed and change the surface pattern across a set of cards.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The design belongs to April Greiman or her client; the photograph’s owner is not stated.
